turns.content: Let property A_n mean that every monic integer polynomial P of degree at most n admits some 1<=k<=n and k+1 distinct integers x1,...,x(k+1) with P(x1)+...+P(xk)=P(xk). Test A_1 using P(x)=x.
For n=2, first consider the constant monic polynomial P(x)=1. Give a valid k and two distinct integer inputs that satisfy the relation.
Still with n=2, let P(c)=x+c be an arbitrary monic linear polynomial. Find k and distinct integers x1,x2,x3 that satisfy the required relation for every integer c.
For an arbitrary monic quadratic P(x)=x^2+a x+b with integer coefficients, construct two distinct integers r and s with P(r)=P(s). Conclude the n=2 verification.

Now let n>=3. Put m=n when n is odd and m=n-1 when n is even, and define F_m(x)=x(x-1)...(x-m+1). For odd n and for even n>=6, justify that F_m(t) is divisible by n for every integer t and define P(x)=F_m(x)+n x+1. Handle n=4 separately with P(x)=x^4+7x^2+4x+1. Verify that each polynomial is monic, has degree at most n, and is congruent to 1 modulo n on every integer input.

Prove that each polynomial from the previous turn is injective on the integers. For the falling-factorial cases use the monotonicity of F_m when m is odd; for n=4 analyze P(x)-P(y). Keep the requirement that all x_i in property A_n are distinct.

Summarize the two features of the polynomial now available for each n>=3: its values are all congruent to 1 modulo n, and it is injective on the integers. Explain why both features matter for obstructing property A_n.
Assume property A_n for one of these polynomials and reduce its required equation modulo n. Use 1<=k<=n, injectivity, and the distinct-input condition to derive a contradiction.
Combine the failure at n=1, the constant, linear, and quadratic cases for n=2, and the obstruction for every n>=3. State all positive integers n satisfying the property.
